KFF's projection assumes current enrollees keep their plans. The increase is $17 a month, or $204 a year, by simple arithmetic on KFF's figures. KFF also reports that no zero-premium stand-alone plans are available in 2027. In its October 30, 2026 release, KFF says people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more. Open enrollment runs through December 7. Tools for this journey Medicare IRMAA Calculator → How Much Medicare Part D 2027 Premiums Rise KFF projects the average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) will rise to $51 in 2027, up 50 percent from $34 in 2026. The projection assumes current enrollees do not switch plans. The arithmetic on KFF's two averages works out as follows: $34 a month in 2026 equals $408 a year. $51 a month in 2027 equals $612 a year. The gap between the two averages is $17 a month, or $204 a year. KFF says more than 4 million people enrolled in zero-premium PDPs will face higher premiums, because no zero-premium PDPs are available in 2027. For Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage (MA-PDs), KFF projects an average of $9 a month in 2027, an increase of less than $2. The $51 figure is an average projection, so a given enrollee may pay more or less. Medicare.gov says Part D premiums vary by plan and may be higher depending on income. Medicare.gov does not list premiums by state or for any individual on the page cited here. No Zero-Premium Stand-Alone Plans in 2027 KFF reports that no zero-premium stand-alone drug plans are available in 2027. KFF's release does not say why plans raised premiums. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) addressed a change to stand-alone plans in a fact sheet dated July 28, 2026. CMS said it will discontinue the voluntary premium stabilization demonstration for stand-alone plans, which began in 2025, at the end of 2026. CMS said plan sponsors had enough experience under the redesigned benefit, so the program returns to traditional market conditions in 2027. CMS does not present the end of the demonstration in the fact sheet as the reason zero-premium plans are absent, and KFF does not offer it as an explanation either. The same CMS fact sheet sets the 2027 national average monthly bid amount at $296.05 and the base beneficiary premium at $41.33. Under the Inflation Reduction Act's premium stabilization provision, the base premium can rise no more than 6 percent per year. Medicare.gov lists the 2026 base beneficiary premium as $38.99, and $38.99 times 1.06 equals $41.33, so by arithmetic the 2027 figure rose by the full 6 percent allowed. What the Lowest- and Highest-Premium National Plans Cost KFF counts eight national PDPs for 2027, with projected average premiums ranging from about $6 to $204 a month. The lowest is Centene 's Wellcare Value Script Rx at $6.50, up from $5.80. The highest is United 's AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00. Plan 2026 Monthly Premium 2027 Projected Monthly Premium 2027 Annual Premium (Arithmetic) Wellcare Value Script Rx (Centene) $5.80 $6.50 $78 AARP Medicare Rx Preferred (United) $126.00 $204.50 $2,454 By arithmetic, the Wellcare plan rises $0.70 a month and the AARP plan rises $78.50 a month. These are average premiums for national plans, and premiums vary by plan. The table covers premiums only, so it does not show what either plan charges as a deductible or for a specific drug. Plans can be compared in Medicare Plan Finder , the Medicare.gov tool for finding and comparing plans. Deductibles and Cost Sharing in Medicare Part D 2027 KFF reports the maximum Part D deductible allowed in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026, and plans may charge less. Medicare.gov lists the same $700 ceiling and notes that some plans have no deductible. Average deductibles and the share of enrollees facing one also rise, according to KFF: PDP enrollees: $643 on average, up from $540. MA-PD enrollees: $489 on average, up from $360. 99.8 percent of PDP enrollees face a deductible if they keep their plans, up from 96 percent. 85 percent of MA-PD enrollees face a deductible if they keep their plans, up from 80 percent. After the deductible, Medicare.gov says enrollees pay 25 percent coinsurance until out-of-pocket spending reaches $2,100 in 2026 or $2,400 in 2027. Once spending reaches that limit, enrollees pay nothing for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. The 2027 limit is $300 higher than the 2026 limit, by arithmetic. KFF says most enrollees will pay coinsurance rather than copayments for preferred and non-preferred drugs, which can make out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Medicare.gov defines a copayment as a fixed dollar amount per prescription and coinsurance as a percentage of the drug cost. A 25 percent coinsurance charge moves with the price of the drug, while a copayment stays the same. How to Compare and Switch Before December 7 Open enrollment runs through December 7, according to KFF, and KFF says relatively low-premium PDP options exist. Medicare Plan Finder at medicare.gov/plan-compare is the Medicare.gov tool for finding and comparing plans. A premium is only part of a plan's yearly cost, because the deductible and coinsurance are added to it. A plan with a lower premium may carry a deductible as high as $700 plus 25 percent coinsurance. A plan with a higher premium may charge a smaller deductible or none. These four items cover the main 2027 drug costs that KFF and Medicare.gov list: The 2027 monthly premium, multiplied by 12 for the annual premium. The deductible, which can be anywhere from $0 to $700. Whether drugs carry coinsurance or copayments after the deductible. The $2,400 out-of-pocket limit, after which covered drugs cost $0 for the rest of 2027. Twelve times the monthly premium plus the deductible is the least a plan costs in a year when the full deductible is paid. Coinsurance on each prescription then adds to that total until out-of-pocket spending reaches $2,400. No source cited publishes any individual's 2027 premium, so each plan's own figures are the numbers to compare. Who Pays Less with Extra Help Extra Help is a Medicare program for people with limited income and resources, according to Medicare.gov's Extra Help page . KFF notes that the 2027 premium increases affect most PDP enrollees who do not receive the extra subsidies provided to low-income enrollees. Medicare.gov lists these 2026 limits: Individual: income of $23,940 and resources of $18,090. Married couple: income of $32,460 and resources of $36,100. Medicare.gov says these limits may rise each year, and Alaska and Hawaii have separate limits that the page does not list. Extra Help is not available in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands or American Samoa. Some people qualify automatically: those with full-benefit Medicaid, those getting state help with Part B premiums through a Medicare Savings Program, and those receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI). Medicare.gov says people can apply for Extra Help and a Medicare Savings Program together. The Medicare Savings Programs guide covers that second program. For 2027, Medicare.gov's Extra Help page describes these costs: Plan premium: $0. Plan deductible: $0. Up to $5.80 per generic drug and up to $14.40 per brand-name drug at participating pharmacies. $0 per covered drug once total drug costs reach $2,400. Medicare.gov says applications go through Social Security online, and free help is available from the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP). Someone who does not qualify now can reapply at any time. If an approved applicant has no Part D plan, Medicare enrolls that person in one. Medicare Advantage Plans with Drug Coverage KFF projects MA-PD premiums will average $9 a month in 2027, up less than $2, and says the stand-alone PDP premium is more than five times higher. That comparison covers average premiums only. MA-PD enrollees face deductibles too. KFF puts the average MA-PD deductible at $489 in 2027, and 85 percent of MA-PD enrollees face one if they keep their plans. Choosing Medicare Advantage is a different decision from choosing a stand-alone drug plan. The Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage comparison covers those differences. Takeaway A stand-alone Part D enrollee who keeps the same plan may see the average increase in KFF's October 30, 2026 projection. The average rise is $17 a month, or $204 a year by arithmetic, and KFF says people facing large increases need to take action to avoid paying significantly more. This applies to stand-alone plan enrollees who do not receive Extra Help, whose plan premium Medicare.gov lists as $0. MA-PD premiums average $9 a month. Keeping the current plan can still be the cheaper choice. If a plan's own 2027 premium, deductible and coinsurance on the enrollee's drugs add up to a lower yearly total than the other plans, staying costs less. A low premium paired with a $700 deductible can cost more over a year than a higher premium with a smaller deductible. Before December 7, you can open Medicare Plan Finder and compare each Medicare Part D 2027 plan's premium together with its deductible and coinsurance. On a $2,000 monthly benefit, that works out to $72 a month before the Medicare Part B premium comes out. Check the Social Security Administration (SSA) COLA page for the official notice. Tools for this journey Social Security COLA calculator → Social Security retirement → Social Security break-even → Retirement calculators → The Official 2027 Social Security COLA Is 3.6% The 2027 Social Security COLA is 3.6%, announced by the SSA on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. The average retired worker gets roughly $75 more a month, and more than 75 million Americans will see the increase, according to CBS News . Payments rise in January 2027, or starting December 31, 2026, for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients. On a $2,000 monthly check, 3.6% adds $72, for a new benefit of $2,072 a month and $864 more over a year. On a $1,500 check, the raise is $54, bringing it to $1,554. To estimate your own raise, multiply your current monthly benefit by 0.036. Medicare has not announced its 2027 premiums, so your net raise is not final. The 2026 Trustees Report projects the standard Part B premium rising $6.60, from $202.90 to $209.50. On the $2,000 example, that leaves $72.00 minus $6.60, or $65.40 a month before other deductions. At 3.6%, this is the largest COLA since 2023, above 3.2% for 2024, 2.5% for 2025, and 2.8% for 2026. It also matches the top of the 3.4% to 3.6% range forecasters published before the announcement. Read the official notice on the SSA COLA page , then enter your new benefit in our Social Security retirement calculator . Forecasts Before the 2027 Social Security COLA Announcement Before the October 14, 2026 announcement, forecasters put the 2027 COLA at roughly 3.4% to 3.6%. Three published numbers made up that range. AARP projected 3.6%, which would have raised the average retired worker's benefit by about $75 a month. The Senior Citizens League projected 3.5%, which 24/7 Wall St. calls "a forecast rather than an official number." 24/7 Wall St. calculated roughly 3.4% if September's CPI-W equals August's reading of 328.481. AARP's forecast uses CPI-W data from October 2025 through August 2026, plus Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projections for September. In August, CPI-W was 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The BLS posted September CPI-W at 8:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, and the official 2027 COLA followed that release. The raise takes effect with January 2027 payments. How the Social Security COLA Is Calculated The Social Security COLA is based on how much CPI-W changes in the third quarter (July, August, and September) compared with the same three months a year earlier. The September CPI-W release is the one that closes out the quarter. Before the announcement, July and August 2026 were already published, and September was the last missing input, so forecasters filled it in. AARP uses a Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projection for that month. 24/7 Wall St. puts the result at roughly 3.4% if the September CPI-W matches August's 328.481. What 3.4%, 3.5%, and 3.6% Look Like on a $2,000 Check The official 3.6% COLA on a $2,000 monthly benefit adds $72 a month, raising the check to $2,072. Over 12 months, that comes to $864 a year. The pre-announcement forecast range moved the result by a few dollars: At 3.4%, $2,000 rises by $68 to $2,068 a month, or $816 a year. At 3.5%, $2,000 rises by $70 to $2,070 a month, or $840 a year. At 3.6% (the official COLA), $2,000 rises by $72 to $2,072 a month, or $864 a year. To estimate your own raise, multiply your current monthly benefit by the percentage. A $1,500 check at 3.6% gains $54 a month. The average retired worker received $2,071 a month after the 2026 COLA. At 3.6%, that average rises by about $74.56, which lines up with AARP's estimate of about $75. You can model your own benefit in our Social Security retirement calculator . Why the Net Raise Can Look Smaller After Medicare Part B Your deposit can rise by less than the COLA because most Medicare Part B enrollees have the premium deducted from their Social Security benefit. When the premium goes up, the increase comes out of the raise. The standard Part B premium was $185.00 in 2025 and is $202.90 in 2026. The 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects $209.50 for 2027, an increase of $6.60, or about 3.3%. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) sets the final amount later. On the $2,000 example, the math runs like this: Gross COLA at 3.6%: +$72.00 a month Part B increase from $202.90 to $209.50: minus $6.60 a month Net monthly gain: $65.40 This is a simplified illustration. It leaves out other deductions, such as taxes on benefits or a Part D premium , and the 2027 premium is not set yet. The hold-harmless rule generally limits your Part B increase to the dollar increase in your Social Security benefit. In the $2,000 example, the $72 raise is much larger than the $6.60 premium increase, so the cap would not apply. The rule does not cover everyone, including new enrollees and some people who pay the income-related amounts. Higher-income enrollees pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) as a surcharge on Part B. In 2026, the surcharge starts above $109,000 of modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for individuals, or $218,000 for married couples filing jointly. About 8% of beneficiaries pay these amounts. 2027 premiums generally use 2025 income. Pull your 2025 tax return and compare your MAGI to those 2026 thresholds to see whether a surcharge could shrink your net raise further. Past Social Security COLAs Compared with the 2027 COLA The official 2027 COLA of 3.6% sits above each of the three prior COLAs. 2024: 3.2% 2025: 2.5% 2026: 2.8% 2027: 3.6% (official) The 2026 COLA of 2.8% took effect in January 2026. It raised the average monthly retired-worker benefit by about $56, from $2,015 to $2,071. Part B rose $17.90 that same year, from $185.00 to $202.90. For someone with the average benefit paying the standard premium, that left a net gain of about $38.10 a month before other deductions. For 2027, the projected Part B increase is $6.60, which takes a smaller share of a larger raise. The 2027 Social Security COLA Notice in Your Online Account To read your 2027 COLA notice online, sign in to your my Social Security account, or create one, and enroll in paperless notices by November 18, 2026. The notice then appears in the account's Message Center in late November, up to three weeks before a paper letter would arrive, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA) press release of October 14 . If you are not enrolled in paperless notices by November 18, the SSA mails your notice in December. Create or sign in to your account at the my Social Security page . Open the Message Center. Choose Preferences and switch your notices to online, or paperless. Turn on text or email alerts if you want a message when a new notice, including the COLA notice, is posted. Open the Message Center in late November to read your notice. The online route changes only when you can read the notice. The 3.6% raise and the January 2027 payment timing are the same whether your letter arrives online or by mail. You can change your notice preference at any time from the Preferences link in the Message Center. If you are enrolled in Medicare, your 2027 premium amount also appears in the Message Center from late November. To estimate your new benefit before the notice arrives, enter your current amount in the Social Security COLA calculator . What to Do Now That the 2027 Social Security COLA Is Announced Now that the official 2027 COLA of 3.6% is out, redo the math on your own check with the real percentage. Open the SSA COLA page and confirm the official percentage. Multiply your current monthly benefit by that percentage to get your gross monthly raise. Subtract the Part B increase. Use the $6.60 Trustees projection until CMS sets the final 2027 premium. If your 2025 MAGI was above the 2026 IRMAA thresholds, a surcharge could raise your premium above the standard amount. Read our guide to whether Social Security is taxable and our list of states that tax Social Security to see what share of the raise you keep after taxes. The $65.40 example fits someone paying the standard Part B premium. If you are a new Medicare enrollee in 2027 or pay income-related amounts, the hold-harmless rule may not apply to you, so redo the subtraction with your own premium. If you have not started benefits yet, compare claiming ages in the Social Security break-even calculator . To see your own 2027 amount, enter your current benefit in the Social Security COLA calculator . For other groups, read how much SSDI goes up in 2027 , the 2027 SSI payment amounts , what the 2027 COLA is for FERS, CSRS and military retirees , and every other 2027 Social Security change . Frequently asked questions How much will Social Security go up in 2027? Social Security benefits go up 3.6% in 2027, the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced on October 14, 2026. The average retired-worker benefit rises by roughly $75 a month, to about $2,170, starting with January 2027 payments. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients see the increase starting December 31, 2026. On a $2,000 monthly benefit, 3.6% adds $72 a month, or $864 a year. When was the 2027 COLA announced? The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, and set it at 3.6%. The raise starts with January 2027 payments, and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients see it starting December 31, 2026. You can read the official figure on the Social Security Administration COLA page . How is the Social Security COLA calculated? The COLA is based on the change in CPI-W for July, August, and September compared with the same three months of the prior year. The official 2027 COLA is 3.6%. Before the announcement, 24/7 Wall St. had estimated roughly 3.4% if September matched August's 328.481. Will Medicare Part B take part of my 2027 raise? Yes, if your Part B premium is deducted from your Social Security benefit. The standard premium is $202.90 in 2026, and the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects $209.50 for 2027, a $6.60 increase. On a $2,000 check with the official 3.6% COLA, that leaves a net gain of $65.40 a month. CMS sets the final premium later, and IRMAA surcharges in 2026 start above $109,000 of MAGI for individuals. What was the 2026 Social Security COLA? The 2026 COLA was 2.8%. It took effect in January 2026 and raised the average monthly retired-worker benefit by about $56, from $2,015 to $2,071. The two COLAs before it were 2.5% for 2025 and 3.2% for 2024. Will my COLA be taxed? It can be. The COLA raises your benefit, and part of Social Security benefits can be taxable. mainEntity.name: How much will Social Security go up in 2027?

acceptedAnswer.text: Social Security benefits go up 3.6% in 2027, the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced on October 14, 2026. The average retired-worker benefit rises by roughly $75 a month, to about $2,170, starting with January 2027 payments. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients see the increase starting December 31, 2026. On a $2,000 monthly benefit, 3.6% adds $72 a month, or $864 a year.

The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, and set it at 3.6%. The raise starts with January 2027 payments, and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients see it starting December 31, 2026. You can read the official figure on the Social Security Administration COLA page.

mainEntity.name: How is the Social Security COLA calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: The COLA is based on the change in CPI-W for July, August, and September compared with the same three months of the prior year. The official 2027 COLA is 3.6%. Before the announcement, 24/7 Wall St. had estimated roughly 3.4% if September matched August's 328.481.

mainEntity.name: Will Medicare Part B take part of my 2027 raise?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your Part B premium is deducted from your Social Security benefit. The standard premium is $202.90 in 2026, and the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects $209.50 for 2027, a $6.60 increase. On a $2,000 check with the official 3.6% COLA, that leaves a net gain of $65.40 a month. CMS sets the final premium later, and IRMAA surcharges in 2026 start above $109,000 of MAGI for individuals.

mainEntity.name: What was the 2026 Social Security COLA?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2026 COLA was 2.8%. It took effect in January 2026 and raised the average monthly retired-worker benefit by about $56, from $2,015 to $2,071. The two COLAs before it were 2.5% for 2025 and 3.2% for 2024.

It can be. The COLA raises your benefit, and part of Social Security benefits can be taxable. See our guide to whether Social Security is taxable for the federal rules and our list of states that tax Social Security for state rules.

Medicare Savings Program: Can Your State Pay Your Part B Premium? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 20, 2026 Yes, your state can pay your Medicare premiums through a Medicare Savings Program if you qualify. The 2026 Part B premium is $202.90 a month, or $2,434.80 over 12 months. There are four Medicare Savings Programs: QMB, SLMB, QI and QDWI. All four go through your state, which decides which program fits you after you apply. The 2026 federal monthly income limits for one person are $1,350 for the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) program, $1,616 for the Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) program, and $1,816 for the Qualifying Individual (QI) program. Tools for this journey Medicare vs Medicaid comparison → How the Four Medicare Savings Programs Pay Your Premiums Medicare.gov's Medicare Savings Programs page lists these 2026 federal limits for all four programs. Program What it pays 2026 monthly income limit (individual / couple) Resource limit (individual / couple) QMB Part A premium (if you lack premium-free Part A), plus Part B premium, deductibles, coinsurance and copayments $1,350 / $1,824 $9,950 / $14,910 SLMB Part B premium only $1,616 / $2,184 $9,950 / $14,910 QI Part B premium $1,816 / $2,455 $9,950 / $14,910 Qualified Disabled and Working Individual (QDWI) Part A premium only $5,405 / $7,299 $4,000 / $6,000 Two programs pay a Part A premium: QMB and QDWI. Part A is premium-free for most people, so this help applies only if you buy Part A, which costs $311 or $565 a month in 2026 depending on how long you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. QDWI is for people who have a disability, are working, and lost their Social Security disability benefits and premium-free Part A because they returned to work. SLMB and QI both require you to have Part A and Part B, and both help pay the Part B premium. QI allows $200 more in monthly income for one person ($1,816 against $1,616). QI also requires a new application every year, and states approve applications first-come, first-served, with priority to people who got QI the previous year. What a Medicare Savings Program Is Worth in 2026 A Medicare Savings Program that pays your Part B premium covers $202.90 a month in 2026, or $2,434.80 over 12 months ($202.90 x 12). The Part B premium can be higher depending on income, and Medicare.gov lists the 2026 figures on its Medicare costs page . QMB pays more than the premium. It also covers Part B deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. The Part B deductible is $283 a year, so the premium plus the deductible comes to $2,717.80 in 2026 ($2,434.80 + $283). Part B coinsurance is usually 20% of the cost of each covered service after the deductible. Under QMB, Medicare providers cannot bill you for that coinsurance on services and items Medicare covers. For someone who has to buy Part A, QMB adds the Part A premium. That premium is $311 or $565 a month, depending on how long you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. The Part A deductible is $1,736 per inpatient hospital benefit period, and the QMB billing rule covers deductibles on Medicare-covered services too. QMB, SLMB and QI members also get Extra Help with prescription drugs. For how stand-alone drug plan premiums are changing in 2027, see our guide to Medicare Part D 2027 premiums . Extra Help means you pay no more than $12.65 in 2026 for each drug covered by your Medicare drug plan, and Medicare.gov's prescription drug cost help page for details. Who Does Not Fit and Where the Limits Bend You may qualify for a Medicare Savings Program in your state even if your income or resources are above the federal limits, because some states do not count certain types or amounts of income or resources. Income limits are also slightly higher in Alaska and Hawaii. QDWI has its own limits. Its income limit is higher, at $5,405 a month for an individual and $7,299 for a couple. Its resource limit is lower, at $4,000 and $6,000, and it only serves working people with a disability who lost premium-free Part A after returning to work. The limits go up each year, so look up the new figures each year on the Medicare Savings Programs page . How to Apply for a Medicare Savings Program Through Your State You apply for a Medicare Savings Program through your state, and the state decides which program or programs you qualify for. Follow these steps: Reach your state. Start from Medicare.gov's talk to someone page to find who to contact. Apply even if you think your income or savings are too high. Medicare.gov says to apply anyway, since some states do not count certain types or amounts of income or resources. Let the state choose the program. Your state determines whether QMB, SLMB, QI or QDWI fits when you apply. If you are placed in QI, mark a date to apply again next year, because QI requires a new application every year. If you are married, use the couple limits when you compare your numbers: $1,824 a month for QMB, $2,184 for SLMB, $2,455 for QI and $7,299 for QDWI. Each program has both an income limit and a resource limit. If you are handling this for a parent, add the application to our elder care planning checklist so a yearly QI reapplication is not missed. What QMB Changes at the Doctor's Office If you qualify for QMB, Medicare providers are not allowed to bill you for services and items Medicare covers, including deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. You may still get a bill for a small Medicaid copayment if one applies. Show your Medicare card and your Medicaid card, or your QMB card, each time you get care. How Medicare Savings Programs Relate to Full Medicaid Medicare Savings Programs and full Medicaid are both run by states, but they are separate programs. Our Medicare vs Medicaid comparison explains how the two programs differ. Because states run the Medicare Savings Programs, your application goes to your state. QI is only available to people who do not qualify for any other Medicaid coverage or benefits. A person turned away from QI for that reason may still qualify for help from another Medicare Savings Program, according to Medicare.gov. For the other ways to get Medicare coverage, see Medicare vs Medicare Advantage and Medicare Advantage vs Medigap . Your next step is to contact your state about a Medicare Savings Program through Medicare.gov's talk to someone page , even if your income is above the figures in the table. Frequently asked questions Do I have to pay for Medicare if I'm on Medicaid? Maybe not, if you qualify for a Medicare Savings Program. Your state then pays your Part B premium, and QMB also pays the Part A premium (if you lack premium-free Part A) plus Part B deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. Your state decides which program applies after you apply. How do I qualify to get my Medicare premium paid? You qualify by applying through your state for a Medicare Savings Program and meeting its income and resource limits. In 2026 the federal monthly income limits for one person are $1,350 for QMB, $1,616 for SLMB and $1,816 for QI, with a $9,950 resource limit. Some states do not count certain income or resources, so apply even if you think you are over. Who pays first if you have Medicare and Medicaid? With QMB, Medicare providers cannot bill you for services and items Medicare covers, apart from a small Medicaid copayment if one applies. For how a specific bill is handled, confirm with your state and your plan through Medicare.gov's talk to someone page . What is the income limit for the Medicare Savings Program in 2026? The 2026 federal monthly income limits are $1,350 for an individual and $1,824 for a couple in QMB, $1,616 and $2,184 in SLMB, $1,816 and $2,455 in QI, and $5,405 and $7,299 in QDWI. Limits are slightly higher in Alaska and Hawaii, and some states do not count certain types of income. Do I have to reapply for a Medicare Savings Program every year? You must reapply every year for QI, and states approve QI first-come, first-served, with priority to people who had QI the year before. For renewal details on any program, ask your state through the talk to someone page . Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions.
